tweets.text: A withdrawal that sends Ether before clearing the caller balance can be withdrawn against again. The balance is still unchanged when control comes back.
Calling another contract hands it control. It can call back into the caller before the first call returns, while state is not yet finalized.
State updates placed after untrusted calls allow repeated execution. That ordering is what makes the callback dangerous.
Reentrancy is not limited to Ether transfers. It can arise from calls to other contracts, and dependencies across multiple contracts also matter.
The fix is checks-effects-interactions: validate inputs and permissions, update the relevant storage state, then make external calls.
In the withdrawal case, save the amount and clear the stored balance with `balances[msg.sender] = 0;` before calling the recipient.
Then require the call to succeed, so a failure reverts the whole operation.
A callback may enter through another function or dependency, so review other callable paths and contracts that share the affected state.
Does any storage write in a function come after a call to another contract, or can a callback reach shared state through a different function?

tweets.text: A loop that pushes Ether to many recipients needs every payment to succeed. One recipient that fails can block the whole operation for everyone.
External calls can fail accidentally or deliberately. When progress depends on every call in a batch succeeding, a single failing call stops all the rest.
The Solidity documentation adds that sending Ether can fail because the recipient runs out of gas, including through require, assert or revert.
With transfer or send plus a return value check, this can give the recipient a way to block progress in the sending contract.
Think of payments pushed to many recipients in a loop: the loop only finishes if each recipient accepts its payment. One refusing recipient blocks the rest.
Isolate each external call into its own transaction that the recipient of the call can initiate. Avoid combining multiple calls in one transaction, especially inside a loop.
For payments, let users withdraw funds instead of pushing funds to them automatically. This also reduces the chance of problems with the gas limit.
Always assume external calls can fail, and write the contract logic to handle a failed call. Pull-style withdrawals keep one recipient's failure from blocking others.
Check your payout code for one condition: does any loop send Ether to a recipient and require that every send succeeds before it can finish?

tweets.text: A lending protocol that values collateral with a price an attacker can move will make liquidation and borrowing decisions on wrong values. That is price oracle manipulation.
An oracle is a trust boundary. The contract implicitly trusts that the price reflects market conditions, and manipulation, staleness or misconfiguration can break that trust.
The protocol trusts price inputs attackers can move. When a price can be influenced directly or indirectly, every decision built on it inherits that weakness.
OWASP lists several forms: spot price manipulation through large trades, flash loans or just-in-time liquidity in the same block, and TWAP manipulation over short windows or low-liquidity periods.
Two more forms: stale or stuck data when freshness is not enforced, and aggregation that fails to reject outliers.
On the input side, aggregate multiple sources with a median or mean and reject outliers. Use TWAPs over sufficient windows and reject prices older than a maximum staleness threshold.
Avoid basing core prices on illiquid pools, and cap the impact of a single pool or feed. Also halt sensitive operations such as borrowing and liquidations on suspicious or unavailable data.
Monitor deviations between the oracle and reference markets with automated alerts. Does any borrow or liquidation path read a price with no staleness check and no cap on a single pool or feed?
